title: Silence is praise (Psalm 65:2)
hook: we can say what God is not better than what God is; "for Thee silence is praise"

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: the torah speaks our language. Words fitted to the listener, like a parent answering a child. When you explained something hard, which words did you reach for? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.

A prayer leader stands before the congregation, and he's on a roll. The prayer has three words for God: great, mighty, awesome. He keeps going. Glorious, powerful, feared, strong, certain, honored. The list grows. In the room sits Rabbi Hanina, and he waits until the man is done. Then he asks him a question, quietly: have you finished all the praises of your Master? The Talmud keeps that question, and Maimonides picks it up in the Guide. Today's word is his answer to it.
screen: `GREAT, MIGHTY, AWESOME.` → `AND MORE, AND MORE.` → `HAVE YOU FINISHED?`

segments.voice: Silence is praise. Turn it four ways. First, the rabbi's point. In the Talmud, Rabbi Hanina goes on: even the three words we say, we would not dare to say if Moses had not used them in the Torah and the sages had not set them in the prayer. Then a parable. It's like a king who owns gold, and people praise him for owning silver. The praise isn't too much. It's too small, and it insults. Second, Maimonides' turn. In the Guide he argues that any positive word we use for God, even a grand one, borrows from our own world and so falls short. What we can do more truly is say what God is not. God is not a body. God is not limited. God is not weak, not ignorant, not made of parts. Each no, he says, brings you a little nearer, the way ruling out what something isn't sharpens what you know. Third, the verse. He reaches for the Psalms. In Hebrew, Psalm sixty-five begins its praise with the words l'kha dumiyah tehillah. Translations differ, and some English versions say praise waits for God. Maimonides reads it as: for You, silence is praise. Not silence as having nothing to say. Silence as the right response once words run out. Fourth, the balance. He doesn't throw out prayer. The fixed words stay, because the Torah and the sages gave them. What he warns against is piling on more, as if more words were more honor. So the prayer is said, and then the silence after it says the rest.
screen: `GOLD PRAISED AS SILVER.` · `SAY WHAT GOD IS NOT.` · `FOR YOU, SILENCE IS PRAISE.` · `SAY THE WORDS, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `SILENCE IS PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Let yourself settle, and take a few slow breaths. If it fits your beliefs, try Maimonides' way for a moment. Say, quietly, one thing God is not. Not a body. Not small. Not far away in the way a person is far away. Let each no stand by itself for a breath. If God isn't part of how you see things, take something vast instead, the sea or the night sky, and say what it isn't. Not a pond. Not a ceiling. Then stop adding words, and simply let the quiet be there. The bell holds the time.
Silence is praise. Maimonides' reading of Psalm sixty-five: since we can say more truly what God is not than what God is, silence becomes a form of praise. Today's word.

Your line: silence is praise. Today, after something moves you, a view, a kindness, a piece of music, don't reach for the adjective. Let one quiet breath say it. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: In the Amidah, which is said quietly, those who pray it praise God as great, mighty and awesome, the words Rabbi Hanina defended. Students of the Guide study Maimonides' teaching on negative attributes in the chapters around 1:58–59.

fork.setup: you're Rabbi Hanina. a prayer leader keeps adding words of praise for God, longer and longer. what do you do?
options: join in and add a few more.
wait, then ask if he's finished all the praises.
fork.reveal: he waits, then asks his question. even the three words we say, he explains, come only because Moses used them.

original.note: Hebrew: silence, stillness. the word in Psalm 65 that Maimonides reads as 'silence is praise'.

trapdoor: what you thought: the more you praise God, the better.
what it means: our positive words fall short; saying what God is not, then going quiet, is more true.
what a scholar hears: Guide 1:59, the doctrine of negative attributes, Rabbi Hanina's story from Berakhot 33b, and dumiyah in Psalm 65:2.

notes: Berakhot 33b paraphrased (Rabbi Hanina, the prayer leader's added praises, the three words from Moses fixed by the Men of the Great Assembly, the king's gold-and-silver parable); the list of extra adjectives is illustrative. Maimonides retells it in Guide 1:59. Please confirm.

Psalm 65:2 not quoted from JPS 1917 (whose rendering is believed to differ, along the lines of 'praise waiteth for Thee'); the Hebrew and Maimonides' reading are given instead, with 'some English versions say praise waits for God'. Please confirm.
